answer.label: Not Yogi Berra — an old joke he explicitly denied
answer.authorName: Unknown (in print by 1876, decades before Berra was born)
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · earliest documented printing 1876 · popularised via Punch, 1911
answer.sourceLine: The joke was circulating in print long before Yogi Berra was born in 1925 — Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to an 1876 novel and a January 1911 Punch cartoon caption. Berra himself denied it twice: to William Safire in 1987 and again in his 1989 autobiography.
answer.confidenceText: No source ties this line to Berra, and he disclaimed it on the record twice.

source.excerpt: IF YOU NEVER GO TO OTHER PEOPLE’S FUNERALS I DON’T SEE HOW YOU CAN EXPECT THEM TO COME TO YOURS.
trail: 1876 — a character in the novel The Youth of the Period says “if I don’t attend other people’s funerals they won’t come to mine,” the earliest citation found by Quote Investigator ↗.
1911 — Punch runs it as a cartoon caption; Wikiquote ↗ cites this as its first unattributed appearance in print, no later than January 1911.
1987 — William Safire phones Berra for his New York Times column “Mr. Bonaprop” and Berra disclaims the line; Safire calls it “not an authentic bonaprop by Berra,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
1989 — Berra puts the denial in his own autobiography Yogi: It Ain’t Over, a book in which he also questions other sayings credited to him, as Quote Investigator ↗ documents.
source.excerptNote: The Punch cartoon caption of 25 January 1911, as transcribed by Quote Investigator — fourteen years before Yogi Berra was born.

source.rightsNote: The modern wording has no identifiable author or first-publication record — it is an anonymous joke that surfaced in many variants, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for this phrasing. The specific early printings that are datable (the 1876 novel, the 1911 Punch caption) are long out of copyright, but they use different words.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.kicker: The name the joke landed on
author.heading: Who Yogi Berra actually was
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra (1925–2015) was a Hall of Fame catcher for the New York Yankees who won ten World Series titles as a player, more than anyone in Major League history. His crooked, paradoxical one-liners became famous enough that unattributed jokes started migrating onto his name — a drift he summed up himself with “I really didn’t say everything I said.” The funeral line is one he specifically refused to claim.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone says Yogi
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook Yogi-ism by adoption: a floating joke with no owner, attached decades later to the most quotable name available.

items.why: Aggregators list it as a Berra quote with no source, edition, or date. Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed and notes it was in print, unattributed, no later than January 1911.
Quote Investigator ↗ records a 1946 LIFE article and a 1973 newspaper column linking the saying to Chicago ward-boss politics — long after the joke was already in print.

Day’s 1935 New Yorker story “Father Plans to Get Out” has “If you don’t go to other men’s funerals, they won’t go to yours,” per Quote Investigator ↗ — but that is 1935, decades after the earliest printings.

misattribution.truthLine: The jest was circulating before Berra was born, and Berra said so himself: “I didn’t say, ‘always go to other people’s funerals; otherwise, they won’t go to yours’” — Yogi: It Ain’t Over (1989), quoted by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: How a Victorian joke became a Yogi-ism
lead: Berra’s real sayings were odd enough to be unmistakable, which made his name a magnet: once a person becomes shorthand for “funny paradox,” ownerless jokes drift onto them. This one had been drifting for a long time already — through a Victorian novel, Cornish dialect stories, a Punch cartoon, Clarence Day in The New Yorker, and Chicago ward-boss lore — before it landed on a Yankees catcher who was not yet born when it first saw print.

What makes this case unusually clean is that the accused denied it. When New York Times language columnist William Safire phoned him in 1987 to check a batch of alleged Yogi-isms, Berra disclaimed the funeral advice; two years later he put the denial in his own book, per Quote Investigator ↗.
context.detailsSummary: Why the trail is hard to follow
detailsBody: The line survives in many wordings — “berrin’s” in Cornish dialect, “other men’s funerals,” “folk’s funerals” — which is why it resisted tracing for so long. Quote Investigator notes the numerous variations across publications and decades as the reason it is difficult to trace.

The version circulating today (“Always go to other people’s funerals; otherwise they won’t go to yours”) is essentially the phrasing Berra quoted in order to reject it — the modern wording is the accusation, not a documented utterance.
context.pull: The joke was in print by 1876. Berra was born in 1925.
